quotes.locator: Book I (Hsiâo-yâo Yû), closing exchange with Hui-dze
quotes.why: The first chapter ends by turning a complaint about uselessness into a question about where and for whom a thing is supposed to be useful.

quotes.text: And there is the great awaking, after which we shall know that this life was a great dream. All the while, the stupid think they are awake, and with nice discrimination insist on their knowledge; now playing the part of rulers, and now of grooms. Bigoted was that Khiû! He and you are both dreaming. I who say that you are dreaming am dreaming myself.
quotes.why: The speaker includes himself in the dream he diagnoses, which is why the passage resists being read as a confident doctrine.

quotes.text: Formerly, I, Kwang Kâu, dreamt that I was a butterfly, a butterfly flying about, feeling that it was enjoying itself I did not know that it was Kâu. Suddenly I awoke, and was myself again, the veritable Kâu. I did not know whether it had formerly been Kâu dreaming that he was a butterfly, or it was now a butterfly dreaming that it was Kâu. But between Kâu and a butterfly there must be a difference. This is a case of what is called the Transformation of Things.
quotes.locator: Book II (Khî Wû Lun), final paragraph
quotes.why: The most quoted story in the book ends not with doubt alone but with the claim that a difference remains, and readers still argue over how the two fit.

quotes.text: What your servant loves is the method of the Tâo, something in advance of any art. When I first began to cut up an ox, I saw nothing but the (entire) carcase. After three years I ceased to see it as a whole. Now I deal with it in a spirit-like manner, and do not look at it with my eyes. The use of my senses is discarded, and my spirit acts as it wills. Observing the natural lines, (my knife) slips through the great crevices and slides through the great cavities, taking advantage of the facilities thus presented.
quotes.why: Cook Ding describes skill as years of practice that end in following the structure already there, and the ruler takes it as a lesson about nourishing life.

quotes.text: Kwang-dze and Hui-dze were walking on the dam over the Hâo, when the former said, 'These thryssas come out, and play about at their ease;--that is the enjoyment of fishes.' The other said, 'You are not a fish; how do you know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?' Kwang-dze rejoined, 'You are not I. How do you know that I do not know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?' Hui-dze said, 'I am not you; and though indeed I do not fully know you, you certainly are not a fish, and (the argument) is complete against your knowing what constitutes the happiness of fishes.' Kwang-dze replied, 'Let us keep to your original question. You said to me, "How do you know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?" You knew that I knew it, and yet you put your question to me;--well, I know it (from our enjoying ourselves together) over the Hâo.'
quotes.why: The logician Hui Shi seems to win the argument, and Zhuangzi answers by shifting the question from proof to the place where knowing happens.

quotes.text: During the intermingling of the waste and dark chaos, there ensued a change, and there was breath; another change, and there was the bodily form; another change, and there came birth and life. There is now a change again, and she is dead. The relation between these things is like the procession of the four seasons from spring to autumn, from winter to summer.
quotes.why: Found drumming and singing after his wife's death, Zhuangzi first admits he was affected, then gives this account of change, and the scene still unsettles readers.

sections.title: Wandering at ease (chapter 1, inner)
sections.keyIdea: Freedom and usefulness look different at different scales.
sections.summary: The book opens with a vast fish that becomes a bird and flies south, while a cicada and a dove laugh at it. Stories of rulers and hermits follow. The chapter ends with Hui Shi's giant gourds and useless tree, which Zhuangzi says are useless only for the purposes Hui Shi has in mind.

sections.title: Making things equal (chapter 2, inner)
sections.keyIdea: Every judgment of right and wrong is made from a standpoint.
sections.summary: Legge titles it "The Adjustment of Controversies"; it is often called the discussion on making all things equal. It moves from the sounds of Earth and Heaven to the disputes of the schools, the monkeys offered three measures of acorns in the morning, the great dream, and the butterfly. It is the most argued-over chapter and the hardest to summarize.

sections.title: Nourishing life and living among people (chapters 3–4, inner)
sections.keyIdea: Skill and survival depend on attention to how things actually are.
sections.summary: Chapter 3 is short and centres on Cook Ding and his knife. Chapter 4 imagines Confucius advising his disciple Yan Hui before a dangerous mission to an unstable ruler, including the practice called fasting of the mind. It closes with more useless trees, including a sacred oak that survives because no carpenter wants it.

sections.title: Virtue, the great teacher, and rulers (chapters 5–7, inner)
sections.keyIdea: Damaged, ugly, or dying bodies do not measure a person's worth.
sections.summary: Chapter 5 presents mutilated and deformed men whose virtue draws others to them. Chapter 6 treats death among friends who sing beside a corpse, and describes the true person of old. Chapter 7 ends the Inner Chapters with Hundun, the faceless emperor of the centre, who dies when well-meaning friends drill seven openings in him.

sections.title: Outer chapters, first group (chapters 8–16)
sections.keyIdea: Later writers extend the critique of imposed morality and government.
sections.summary: Chapters 8 to 10 attack Confucian benevolence and righteousness as damage to natural endowment, using images such as webbed toes and horses' hoofs. The following chapters mix this polemic with discussion of how a ruler should govern by not interfering. Scholars such as A. C. Graham assign these chapters to several later schools, though the groupings are debated.

sections.title: Outer chapters, second group (chapters 17–22)
sections.keyIdea: Stories and dialogues develop the Inner Chapters' themes of perspective and death.
sections.summary: Chapter 17 opens with the River Earl discovering the size of the ocean and ends with the fish at the Hao river. Chapter 18 contains the death of Zhuangzi's wife and his conversation with a skull. Chapters 19 to 22 add skill stories and dialogues on knowing the Dao, and some scholars read this group as close in spirit to the Inner Chapters.

sections.title: Miscellaneous chapters (chapters 23–33)
sections.keyIdea: The final chapters are the most varied in date, voice, and viewpoint.
sections.summary: This section mixes dialogues, fragments, and essays. Chapters 28 to 31, including the story of Robber Zhi rebuking Confucius, have long been suspected by Chinese critics of being later additions. Chapter 33 surveys the thinkers of the age, Zhuangzi among them, and is often read as an early history of Chinese philosophy.

faq.q: Which translation of the Zhuangzi should I read?
faq.a: James Legge (1891) and Herbert Giles (1889) are public domain and complete, though their English is dated and Legge spells the name Kwang-dze. Burton Watson's Complete Works of Zhuangzi and Brook Ziporyn's translations are widely used modern choices. A. C. Graham's Chuang-tzu: The Inner Chapters rearranges the text according to his theory of its layers, which is useful but contested.

faq.q: Did Zhuangzi write the whole book?
faq.a: Probably not. Most scholars hold that the seven Inner Chapters are closest to Zhuang Zhou himself, while the Outer and Miscellaneous Chapters include work by followers and other writers. The received 33-chapter text goes back to the edition of Guo Xiang in the 3rd–4th century CE, who is reported to have cut down a longer 52-chapter version. Even the Inner Chapters' authorship is debated.

faq.q: Where should a beginner start, and how long is it?
faq.a: Start with the seven Inner Chapters, which take about three to four hours to read. Chapters 17 and 18 are good next steps because they contain the fish at the Hao and the death of Zhuangzi's wife. The complete text runs to roughly the length of a long novel.

faq.q: What does the butterfly dream mean?
faq.a: Readers disagree. Some take it as a sceptical point about whether we can tell dreaming from waking; others stress its last lines, which insist that a difference remains and present the dream as a case of things changing into one another. Legge's note compares it to the Buddhist idea of illusion, a comparison many later scholars reject for this passage.

practice.title: Read one argument from both sides
practice.instruction: Read the dialogue at the Hao river (Book XVII, paragraph 13) twice. On the first reading, write in one line what Hui-dze claims and why his logic seems sound. On the second, write in one line what Kwang-dze claims, and mark the exact point where he changes the meaning of the question "how do you know". Then write one sentence naming the certainty the story makes harder to hold, and one sentence on whether you think Kwang-dze answered or evaded Hui-dze.

facts.origin: Core material associated with Zhuang Zhou (traditionally c. 369–286 BCE), Warring States China; other chapters added by later hands, probably by the 2nd century BCE; received text edited by Guo Xiang (d. 312 CE)
facts.firstRead: 3–4 hours for the Inner Chapters; 12–15 hours for the complete text

translation.translator: None available in the public domain
translation.title: Vijñānabhairava, Sanskrit text with the commentaries of Kṣemarāja and Śivopādhyāya, ed. Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī (Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, no. 8)
translation.rightsNote: No English translation that is public domain worldwide is known. The first English translation made from the Sanskrit is Jaideva Singh's Vijñānabhairava, or Divine Consciousness (1979), and the widely read adaptation "Centering", in Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (1957) compiled by Paul Reps and Nyogen Senzaki, is also in copyright; Christopher Wallis's translation is current work. Quotations are therefore omitted. Verse pointers below follow the numbering of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies Sanskrit edition (1918), which Singh also uses; other editions can differ by a verse or two.

sections.title: The frame dialogue (vv. 1–23)
sections.keyIdea: Bhairavi asks what Bhairava's true nature is, and he answers that it lies beyond every ritual form.
sections.summary: The goddess Bhairavi says she has heard the teachings of the Rudrayamala Tantra yet her doubts remain. She asks whether the highest reality is sound, the phases of the Trika system, the energies, or something else. Bhairava replies that these are aids for the immature and that his real nature is a state free of all such designations. She then asks how that state can be reached, which introduces the practices.

sections.title: Breath and the pause between breaths (c. vv. 24–27)
sections.keyIdea: Attention rests at the points where breath turns.
sections.summary: The first dharanas take the incoming and outgoing breath as their object. They direct attention to the two points where breath arises and dissolves, and to the pause when breath is held. Breath returns later in the text as well, for example in the closing verses on the natural repetition of breath.

sections.title: Rising energy and the centres of the body (c. vv. 28–31)
sections.keyIdea: Visualizations of energy ascending through the body.
sections.summary: Several dharanas describe energy rising like lightning from centre to centre, up to and beyond the crown of the head. These verses draw on the subtle-body vocabulary of the wider Shaiva Tantric tradition. Commentators link them with kundalini, though the term itself is used sparingly.

sections.title: Closing the senses, sound, and mantra (c. vv. 32–42)
sections.keyIdea: Inner light, unstruck sound, and syllables that fade into silence.
sections.summary: Some practices close the openings of the senses and attend to the inner field that remains. Others take sound as the object: the unstruck inner sound, the syllable Om, a sound followed until it dies away, and the lingering tone of a stringed instrument. The common structure is to follow a sound to its end and remain there.

sections.title: Space and emptiness (c. vv. 43–60)
sections.keyIdea: The body and the world contemplated as empty space.
sections.summary: A long run of dharanas asks the practitioner to contemplate the body, its skin, or all directions at once as void. Others dissolve the body in imagined fire or contemplate the world as if it were burning away. These verses are the source of many modern summaries of the text as a manual of space meditation.

sections.title: Gaps and edges of experience (scattered, e.g. c. vv. 61, 118)
sections.keyIdea: The moment between two perceptions or at the edge of a strong event.
sections.summary: Several practices point to transitions: the gap between two thoughts or two perceptions, the start of a sneeze, or the moment of fear, grief, or sudden surprise. The text treats these moments as openings where ordinary mental activity briefly stops. They are spread through the text rather than gathered in one block.

sections.title: Pleasure, emotion, and ordinary life (c. vv. 68–138)
sections.keyIdea: Everyday sensations and feelings used as supports for contemplation.
sections.summary: A notable group uses pleasure as a support: the memory of sexual union, the joy of meeting a long-absent friend, the taste of food and drink, and absorption in music. Later dharanas turn to looking at the open sky, lying in darkness, swaying on a swing, or noticing desire and anger as they arise. The practices end at about verse 138, completing the traditional count of 112, although scholars note the count is not exact.

sections.title: The closing teaching (c. vv. 139–163)
sections.keyIdea: Ritual terms are redefined as inner recognition, and the dialogue ends.
sections.summary: Bhairava explains that repetition of mantra, meditation, worship, oblation, and pilgrimage are, in their real sense, forms of this same recognition. He describes the natural repetition of breath as a mantra that goes on by itself. Bhairavi, satisfied, embraces Bhairava, and the text closes.

faq.q: Is there a free English translation of the Vijnana Bhairava Tantra?
faq.a: No English translation is known to be in the public domain worldwide. Jaideva Singh's 1979 translation with commentary was the first made from the Sanskrit and is still widely used; Paul Reps's 1957 "Centering" is a loose adaptation rather than a translation. The Sanskrit text itself was published in 1918 in the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.

faq.q: What does "Vijnana Bhairava" mean?
faq.a: Bhairava is a fierce form of Shiva, and in this text the name stands for ultimate reality. Vijnana means consciousness or awareness, so the title is often rendered "the Bhairava of consciousness" or "consciousness as Bhairava". Translators differ on the exact nuance.

faq.q: How old is the Vijnana Bhairava Tantra?
faq.a: It presents itself as part of the Rudrayamala Tantra, but that attribution is traditional, not historical. Scholars usually place its composition between the 7th and 9th centuries CE, probably in Kashmir or elsewhere in northern India, and it was known to Abhinavagupta's circle by around 1000 CE. Dating remains uncertain.

faq.q: Are there really 112 meditations?
faq.a: The number 112 comes from the traditional reckoning of the dharanas between about verse 24 and verse 138. Counting depends on how verses are divided, and some verses contain more than one practice while others restate earlier ones. Translators and commentators arrive at slightly different lists.

practice.title: Map the question before the answers
practice.instruction: Using a named translation such as Jaideva Singh's, read verses 1–23 slowly. Write down each thing Bhairavi asks about, in the order she asks, and next to it the reason Bhairava gives for setting it aside. Then read one practice from three different groups in this map, for example one on breath, one on sound, and one on an everyday experience. For each, write one line on what it takes as its object and where it asks attention to rest. Keep this as a reading exercise; the guide is a map of the text, not instruction in practice.

facts.origin: Composed c. 7th–9th century CE (dating contested); Shaiva Tantric tradition, probably Kashmir or northern India
facts.form: About 163 verses: a frame dialogue, 112 contemplative practices (dharanas), and a closing teaching
facts.firstRead: 1–2 hours for the verses in translation

translation.title: Confucian Analects (The Chinese Classics, vol. 1)
translation.rightsNote: First published 1861; revised second edition 1893, the text given on sacred-texts.com. Translator died 1897. Public domain worldwide. Passage numbers follow Legge's book and chapter divisions, which differ by one in places from some modern editions.

quotes.text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
quotes.why: The collection opens with three questions that tie study, friendship, and indifference to reputation into one picture of a cultivated person.

quotes.text: At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven. At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.
quotes.why: Confucius describes his own life as decades of practice, ending where desire and right conduct no longer pull apart.

quotes.text: Yu, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;-this is knowledge.
quotes.why: Addressed to the bold disciple Zilu, it defines knowledge partly as an honest account of its own limits.

quotes.text: The Master standing by a stream, said, "It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!"
quotes.why: Commentators have read this single image as a lament for passing time and as praise of unceasing effort, and the text leaves both open.

quotes.text: Chi Lu asked about serving the spirits of the dead. The Master said, "While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?" Chi Lu added, "I venture to ask about death?" He was answered, "While you do not know life, how can you know about death?"
quotes.why: Confucius turns a question about spirits and death back to the duties of the living, a deflection readers still argue over.

quotes.text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, "Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?" The Master said, "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
quotes.why: The term Legge renders as reciprocity (shu) is given a negative formulation here, which the text also uses in answer to Zhonggong at XII.2.

sections.title: Learning and filial conduct (books I–II)
sections.keyIdea: Character is formed through study, family duty, and trustworthy speech.
sections.summary: The opening books set the vocabulary of the collection: learning, filial piety, sincerity, and self-examination. Disciples such as Master You and Master Zeng speak alongside Confucius. Book II adds government by virtue, compared to the pole star, and Confucius's short autobiography.

sections.title: Ritual and humaneness (books III–IV)
sections.keyIdea: Ritual form matters only when it carries real feeling and humaneness.
sections.summary: Book III criticizes leading ministerial families for taking ritual and music that are not theirs, and asks what ritual is without humaneness behind it. Book IV gathers sayings on ren, often translated as humaneness or perfect virtue, and on the contrast between the superior man and the small man.

sections.title: Disciples, contemporaries, and the Master's self-portrait (books V–VIII)
sections.keyIdea: Ethical ideals are tested against named people and their conduct.
sections.summary: Books V and VI assess disciples and public figures, often briefly and sometimes sharply. Book VII collects Confucius's descriptions of himself as a transmitter and lover of antiquity rather than an originator. Book VIII includes sayings of Master Zeng and praise of the ancient sage kings.

sections.title: The Master in person (books IX–X)
sections.keyIdea: The text shows Confucius's manner as well as his teaching.
sections.summary: Book IX records remarks by and about Confucius, including the image of the stream. Book X is different in kind: it describes his dress, diet, and bearing at court and at home, detail by detail. Readers who expect doctrine often find Book X the strangest part of the collection.

sections.title: Humaneness, government, and the disciples (books XI–XV)
sections.keyIdea: Personal cultivation and political order are treated as one continuous task.
sections.summary: Book XI centres on the disciples, especially Confucius's grief at the death of Yan Hui. Books XII and XIII answer questions about ren and about governing, including the rectification of names. Books XIV and XV range over recluses, ministers, and rulers, and include the rule of reciprocity.

sections.title: Later layers (books XVI–XX)
sections.keyIdea: The final books differ in form and are often read as later additions.
sections.summary: Book XVI groups sayings into numbered sets and introduces each with the formal heading "Confucius said" rather than "The Master said". Book XVIII records encounters with recluses who mock Confucius's efforts, Book XIX gives the sayings of disciples, and Book XX closes with speeches of the ancient kings. Many scholars treat these books as later strata, though the extent and order of accretion is debated.

faq.q: Which translation of the Analects should I read?
faq.a: James Legge's 1861 and 1893 translation is public domain and closely literal, with archaic phrasing and Victorian terms such as "superior man". Modern complete translations by D. C. Lau, Edward Slingerland, and David Hinton read more easily, and Slingerland adds traditional commentary. Comparing two translations on key terms such as ren and li is more useful than trusting one.

faq.q: Did Confucius write the Analects?
faq.a: No. The Analects records sayings and conversations attributed to Confucius and his disciples, compiled by later followers. Most scholars date its compilation across several generations after his death in 479 BCE, with the received text settled in the Han dynasty. How early each book is remains contested.

faq.q: How long is the Analects, and where should a beginner start?
faq.a: It has 20 short books and roughly 500 passages, most only a few lines long. Books I, II, IV, and XII give a good first sample of its main terms. Reading the whole text straight through takes about four to six hours.

faq.q: Is the Analects a religious scripture?
faq.a: It has been a canonical classic of Confucian tradition, memorized for the imperial examinations and honoured in temple ritual. It contains little doctrine about gods or an afterlife, and Book XI deliberately turns questions about spirits back to human duties. Whether Confucianism is best described as a religion is itself a scholarly debate.

practice.title: Trace one word across the text
practice.instruction: Read Book IV, chapters 1 to 7, and Book XII, chapters 1 to 3, where the word Legge translates as "perfect virtue" (ren) appears repeatedly. On a sheet with two columns, write down each thing a passage says ren is and each thing it says ren is not. Then note who is being answered in Book XII and how the answer changes with the questioner. End by writing one sentence on what the answers have in common, without importing a modern definition.

facts.origin: Compiled by followers of Confucius over several generations after 479 BCE, in the state of Lu and beyond; received text fixed in the Han dynasty (dating of individual books is debated)
facts.form: 20 books of short sayings and dialogues, about 500 passages in all

translation.title: Tattvarthadhigama Sutra: A Treatise on the Essential Principles of Jainism (Sacred Books of the Jainas, vol. II)
translation.rightsNote: Published at Arrah in 1920; translator Jagmandar Lal Jaini died 1927. Public domain worldwide. Quotes are taken from the text layer of the Digital Library of India scan on archive.org. That scan's text layer carries clean English only for chapter 1, so later sutras such as 5.21 (parasparopagraho jivanam) are described in the FAQ but not quoted. The third quote is Jaini's own editorial note, not a sutra.

quotes.text: Right belief, (right) knowledge, (right) conduct, these (together constitute) the path to liberation
quotes.why: The opening sutra names the three jewels together, and Jaini's commentary insists that liberation needs all three at once rather than any one alone.

quotes.text: Belief or conviction in things ascertained as they are, (is) right belief.
quotes.why: Right belief is defined as conviction about the categories of reality, so faith in this text depends on the definitions that follow.

quotes.text: The following seven are known as the seven tattvas or principles Jiva (soul), Ajiva (non-soul) Asrava (inflow of matter into soul), Bandha (bondage of soul by matter), Samvara (stoppage of inflow of matter into soul), Nirjara (shedding of matter by the soul) and Moksa (liberation of soul from matter)
quotes.locator: Jaini's note 2 to the invocatory verses before chapter 1, sutra 1 (the seven tattvas listed in sutra 1.4)
quotes.why: This editor's gloss lays out the seven principles that the rest of the sutra works through chapter by chapter, from soul to liberation.

sections.title: The path and the means of knowing (chapter 1)
sections.keyIdea: Liberation requires right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct together.
sections.summary: The chapter names the three jewels and the seven tattvas. It sets out how things are to be examined, through the standpoints (nayas) and valid means of knowledge. It then classifies the five kinds of knowledge, from sensory knowledge to the omniscience (kevala) of the liberated.

sections.title: The soul (chapter 2)
sections.keyIdea: The soul is defined by consciousness and classified by its condition and senses.
sections.summary: Chapter 2 lists the soul's dispositions (bhavas) according to how karma is subsided, destroyed, or operating. It gives consciousness (upayoga) as the soul's defining mark. It then classifies living beings from one-sensed beings such as plants up to five-sensed beings with mind, and describes their bodies and kinds of birth.

sections.title: The lower, middle, and celestial worlds (chapters 3–4)
sections.keyIdea: Souls are placed within a detailed map of the universe.
sections.summary: Chapter 3 describes the seven hells and the lifespans of their beings, then the concentric continents and oceans of the middle world where humans live. Chapter 4 describes the four orders of celestial beings, their dwellings, and their lifespans. Readers often find these cosmological chapters the least familiar part of the text.

sections.title: Non-soul substances (chapter 5)
sections.keyIdea: Reality consists of eternal substances, each with its own function.
sections.summary: Chapter 5 treats the non-soul (ajiva) substances: the media of motion and rest, space, matter, and time, whose status some commentators discuss. It assigns each substance a function, and at 5.21 says that the function of souls is to support one another. It ends by defining substance through its qualities and modes.

sections.title: The inflow of karma (chapter 6)
sections.keyIdea: Activity of body, speech, and mind draws karmic matter into the soul.
sections.summary: Chapter 6 defines yoga as activity of body, speech, and mind, and asrava as the inflow of karma it causes. It distinguishes inflow driven by passions from inflow without them. It then lists the kinds of conduct that attract each type of karma.

sections.title: The vows (chapter 7)
sections.keyIdea: Nonviolence heads the vows that restrain the inflow of karma.
sections.summary: Chapter 7 sets out the five vows of nonviolence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and non-possession, in their complete form for mendicants and a partial form for laypeople. It defines injury as harm to life caused through careless or passion-driven activity. It adds supplementary lay vows and discusses the end-of-life fast (sallekhana).

sections.title: Bondage (chapter 8)
sections.keyIdea: Karma binds the soul in kinds, durations, intensities, and quantities.
sections.summary: Chapter 8 names the causes of bondage, including wrong belief, non-restraint, carelessness, passions, and activity. It lists the eight main types of karma and their subtypes. It then sets out how long each type can remain bound and how strongly it takes effect.

sections.title: Stoppage, shedding, and liberation (chapters 9–10)
sections.keyIdea: Restraint stops new karma, austerity removes old karma, and the freed soul rises.
sections.summary: Chapter 9 describes stoppage (samvara) through restraints, carefulness, ten virtues, twelve reflections, and the endurance of hardships, and shedding (nirjara) through outer and inner austerities, including meditation. Chapter 10 describes omniscience following the destruction of deluding karma, then liberation (moksha). The liberated soul rises to the summit of the universe.

faq.q: Do Svetambara and Digambara Jains both accept the Tattvartha Sutra?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the few doctrinal texts accepted by both major Jain traditions, which is part of its authority. The two transmit different recensions that differ in the number and wording of some sutras. Svetambaras read it with a commentary (Bhashya) they ascribe to Umasvati, while Digambaras call the author Umasvami and read it with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi; the authorship of the Bhashya is disputed.

faq.q: Which translation should I read?
faq.a: J. L. Jaini's 1920 translation is public domain and gives the Sanskrit, a word-by-word gloss, and notes, though its English is dated. Nathmal Tatia's That Which Is (1994) translates the sutras with the combined commentaries of Umasvati, Pujyapada, and Siddhasenagani, and marks differences between recensions. Vijay K. Jain's 2018 edition gives the Digambara text with the Sarvarthasiddhi.

faq.q: What does "parasparopagraho jivanam" mean?
faq.a: It is sutra 5.21, usually translated as "souls render service to one another" or "the function of souls is to help one another". In context it is one of a series of sutras naming what each substance does, alongside matter's role in pleasure, pain, life, and death. It has become a widely used modern Jain motto, and was adopted with the Jain emblem in 1974.

faq.q: How long is it, and where should a beginner start?
faq.a: It has about 350 short sutras in ten chapters; the Digambara recension counts 357 and the Svetambara slightly fewer. The sutras alone can be read in one or two hours, but they are written to be read with commentary. Chapter 1 sets out the framework, chapter 5 the substances, and chapter 7 the ethical vows.

practice.title: Build the seven-principle glossary
practice.instruction: Read chapter 1, sutras 1 to 4, with the translator's notes. Write the seven tattvas in a column, and beside each write in plain words what process or entity it names, using only the translator's definitions. Then read the opening of chapter 7 on the vows, and mark which of the seven principles nonviolence is meant to affect. Close by writing one sentence on why the text defines these terms before it gives any ethical rule.

facts.origin: Composed in Sanskrit by Umasvati (Umasvami in Digambara usage), India; proposed dates range from the 2nd to the 5th century CE
facts.form: About 350 aphorisms (sutras) in 10 chapters; counts differ between the Svetambara and Digambara recensions
facts.firstRead: 1–2 hours for the sutras alone; several weeks with a commentary

translation.translator: L. H. Mills (Yasna and Gathas); James Darmesteter (Vendidad and Yashts)
translation.title: The Zend-Avesta (Sacred Books of the East, vols. 4, 23 and 31)
translation.rightsNote: Darmesteter's volumes appeared in 1880 (vol. 4, Vendidad) and 1883 (vol. 23, Sirozahs, Yashts and Nyayish); Mills' vol. 31 (Yasna, Visperad, Afrinagan, Gahs) appeared in 1887. Darmesteter died in 1894 and Mills in 1918, so these translations are public domain worldwide. Mills' Gatha renderings are dense and much of his interpretation is now contested; modern readers of the Gathas usually turn to Stanley Insler (1975), Helmut Humbach (1991) or Prods Oktor Skjærvø, whose translations are in copyright and are not quoted here.

quotes.text: Thus are the primeval spirits who as a pair (combining their opposite strivings), and (yet each) independent in his action, have been famed (of old). (They are) a better thing, they two, and a worse, as to thought, as to word, and as to deed. And between these two let the wisely acting choose aright. (Choose ye) not (as) the evil-doers!
quotes.why: This is the passage behind every summary of Zoroastrian dualism, and it frames the two spirits as a choice set before the listener rather than as a finished cosmology.

quotes.text: This I ask Thee, O Ahura! tell me aright: Who by generation was the first father of the Righteous Order (within the world)? Who gave the (recurring) sun and stars their (undeviating) way? Who established that whereby the moon waxes, and whereby she wanes, save Thee? These things, O Great Creator! would I know, and others likewise still.
quotes.why: Yasna 44 is built from repeated questions put to Ahura Mazda, and this verse shows the Gathas praying by asking rather than by asserting.

quotes.text: As the Ahû is excellent, so is the Ratu (one who rules) from (his) sanctity, a creator of mental goodness, and of life's actions done for Mazda; and the Kingdom (is) for Ahura, which to the poor may offer a nurturer.
quotes.locator: Yasna 27.13, the Ahuna Vairya (Yatha Ahu Vairyo), tr. Mills
quotes.why: This is the most recited Zoroastrian prayer, and Mills' bracketed, halting English shows how hard its compressed Avestan syntax is to carry over.

quotes.text: He who sows corn, sows holiness: he makes the law of Mazda grow higher and higher: he makes the law of Mazda as fat as he can with a hundred acts of adoration, a thousand oblations, ten thousand sacrifices.
quotes.why: The Vendidad treats farming as a religious act, and this line sets tilling the ground on the same scale as worship.

quotes.text: For that deed there is nothing that can pay, nothing that can atone, nothing that can cleanse from it; it is a trespass for which there is no atonement, for ever and ever.
quotes.why: The same chapter that praises the farmer ends with penalties for burying a corpse in the earth, and a reader should see how purity law and cosmic struggle are bound together in this book.

quotes.text: And when the sun rises up, then the earth, made by Ahura, becomes clean; the running waters become clean, the waters of the wells become clean, the waters of the sea become clean, the standing waters become clean; all the holy creatures, the creatures of the Good Spirit, become clean.
quotes.why: This short hymn to the sun belongs to the daily prayers of the Khordeh Avesta, and it shows the later Avesta's concern with light, water and cleanliness in concrete terms.

sections.title: Yasna (72 chapters)
sections.keyIdea: The core liturgy recited by priests during the high ritual of the same name.
sections.summary: The Yasna is the text of the principal Zoroastrian act of worship, performed by priests with the preparation and offering of haoma. Its 72 chapters (haiti) combine invocations, confessions of faith and hymns. The Gathas and other Old Avestan pieces sit inside it, so the oldest material survives as part of a living ritual rather than as a separate book.

sections.title: The Gathas (Yasna 28–34, 43–51, 53)
sections.keyIdea: Seventeen hymns in Old Avestan, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra.
sections.summary: The seventeen Gathas are arranged in five groups by metre: Ahunavaiti, Ushtavaiti, Spentamainyu, Vohukhshathra and Vahishtoishti. They address Ahura Mazda directly and speak of truth (asha), the lie (druj), good mind and the choice each person makes. Their language is archaic and their syntax compressed, which is why translations differ sharply. The Yasna Haptanghaiti (Yasna 35–41), in the same Old Avestan dialect, is usually studied alongside them.

sections.title: Visperad
sections.keyIdea: Supplementary liturgy that extends the Yasna for seasonal festivals.
sections.summary: The Visperad ("all the lords") is a set of additional invocations inserted into the Yasna service, especially for the six seasonal festivals (gahambars). It is not read on its own in ritual practice. Mills translated it in the same SBE volume as the Yasna.

sections.title: Vendidad (22 fargards)
sections.keyIdea: Law against the demons: purity, penalties, and a cosmology of the good creation.
sections.summary: The Vendidad (videvdad, "law against the daevas") opens with a list of lands created by Ahura Mazda and the story of Yima, then turns to purity law, the handling of the dead, penalties and the care of dogs and the earth. Fargard 3, on what gladdens and grieves the earth, praises cultivation and forbids burying corpses. It is in Younger Avestan and is generally dated later than the Gathas, though scholars disagree about when it was compiled.

sections.title: Yashts (21 hymns)
sections.keyIdea: Hymns to individual yazatas, the beings worthy of worship.
sections.summary: The Yashts praise figures such as Mithra, Anahita, Tishtrya (Sirius) and the fravashis, and several preserve old Iranian myth and epic material. Some are long and narrative; others, like the Khorshed Yasht to the sun, are brief. Darmesteter translated them in SBE vol. 23 together with the Sirozahs and Nyayish.

sections.title: Khordeh Avesta
sections.keyIdea: The "little Avesta" of prayers used by lay Zoroastrians.
sections.summary: The Khordeh Avesta is a prayer book drawn from the wider corpus for daily and household use. It gathers short formulas such as the Ashem Vohu and the Ahuna Vairya, the five Nyayish, the Gah prayers for the times of day, the Sirozah and selected Yashts. Its contents vary between editions and between Parsi and Iranian communities.

sections.title: Survival and loss of the corpus
sections.keyIdea: What exists today is a fraction of a larger Sasanian canon, preserved mainly through ritual use.
sections.summary: The texts were transmitted orally for many centuries and written down in a purpose-built Avestan script, probably in the Sasanian period (c. 5th–6th century CE). Middle Persian sources, especially the Denkard, describe a Sasanian Avesta of 21 books (nasks), of which only part survives; a common estimate is about a quarter. The surviving manuscripts are late, the oldest dating from around the 13th–14th centuries CE, and what survived is largely what was recited in worship.

faq.q: Which translation of the Avesta should I read?
faq.a: For the Gathas, most readers now use a modern scholarly translation such as those by Stanley Insler, Helmut Humbach or Prods Oktor Skjærvø, since they rest on better linguistic knowledge than the Victorian versions. The Sacred Books of the East volumes by Mills and Darmesteter remain the only complete English Avesta that is freely available, and they are useful for the Vendidad and Yashts. Whichever you use, note the section and the translator, because renderings of the same verse can differ widely.

faq.q: Did Zarathustra write the Avesta?
faq.a: Zoroastrian tradition attributes the Gathas to Zarathustra, and most scholars accept that they come from him or from his immediate circle. The rest of the Avesta was composed later by many hands over a long period. His dates are disputed: estimates range from before 1000 BCE to around the 6th century BCE, with many specialists favouring the earlier range on linguistic grounds.

faq.q: Where should a beginner start with the Avesta?
faq.a: Start with a few Gathas, such as Yasna 30 and Yasna 44, read slowly with notes. Then read Vendidad Fargard 3 and one short Yasht, such as the Khorshed Yasht, to see how the later texts differ in language and concern. Keep in mind that these are liturgical texts recited in Avestan, not books written to be read silently in translation.

faq.q: Is the Avesta the same as the Zend-Avesta?
faq.a: "Zend-Avesta" is an older European name that joins Avesta (the scripture) and Zand (its Middle Persian commentary and translation). Scholars now prefer to call the scripture simply the Avesta. Middle Persian works such as the Bundahishn and Denkard are a separate body of religious literature, even though they draw on the Avesta.

practice.title: Reading the choice in Yasna 30
practice.instruction: Read Yasna 30.1–30.6 in Mills' translation. Then copy verse 3 by hand, leaving out every word Mills placed in brackets, and read the shorter version aloud. Write down which bracketed words changed the meaning most, and what the verse asks the listener to do. If you have access to a modern translation, compare verse 3 and note one place where the two disagree.

facts.origin: Gathas usually dated c. 1500–1000 BCE, though some scholars argue for later dates; the Younger Avesta was composed over the following centuries in eastern Iran; written down c. 5th–6th century CE
facts.language: Avestan (Old Avestan for the Gathas and Yasna Haptanghaiti; Younger Avestan for most of the rest)
facts.form: A liturgical corpus: Yasna (72 chapters, including 17 Gathas), Visperad, Vendidad (22 fargards), 21 Yashts and the Khordeh Avesta
facts.firstRead: 2–3 hours for the Gathas with notes; 15–20 hours for the full SBE translation

translation.translator: Bahá’í World Centre (incorporating translations by Shoghi Effendi)
translation.title: The Kitáb-i-Aqdas: The Most Holy Book (authorized English translation)
translation.rightsNote: The authorized English translation (1992) is in copyright. The Bahá’í Reference Library legal page (bahai.org/legal, last updated 5 September 2022) states that all site content is protected by copyright; it permits use provided the content is not used in a way that misrepresents the intent of the original source and is accompanied by the notice “Copyright © Bahá’í International Community” with attribution; commercial use requires prior permission (termsofuse@bahai.org); and permission may be withdrawn at any time. Four short excerpts (each under 40 words) are quoted here with paragraph locators and attribution: © Bahá’í International Community. No public-domain English translation of the whole book exists.

quotes.text: These twin duties are inseparable. Neither is acceptable without the other.
quotes.why: The opening paragraph ties recognition of Bahá’u’lláh to observance of His laws, and this pairing governs how the rest of the book asks to be read. © Bahá’í International Community.

quotes.text: Think not that We have revealed unto you a mere code of laws. Nay, rather, We have unsealed the choice Wine with the fingers of might and power.
quotes.why: The book describes itself here, and the image of wine rather than statute tells the reader to take its laws as devotional as well as legal. © Bahá’í International Community.

quotes.text: Say: O leaders of religion! Weigh not the Book of God with such standards and sciences as are current amongst you, for the Book itself is the unerring Balance established amongst men.
quotes.why: This passage addresses religious scholars and sets the text as its own measure, which is a demanding claim for any outside reader to keep in view. © Bahá’í International Community.

quotes.text: Consort with all religions with amity and concord, that they may inhale from you the sweet fragrance of God. Beware lest amidst men the flame of foolish ignorance overpower you.
quotes.why: This command shapes Bahá’í relations with other faiths and sits alongside the book's abolition of earlier notions of ritual uncleanness (¶ 75). © Bahá’í International Community.

sections.title: Preface, introduction and Shoghi Effendi's description
sections.keyIdea: The authorized edition first explains what the book is and how it is applied.
sections.summary: The volume opens with a preface and an introduction by the Universal House of Justice, followed by a description of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas by Shoghi Effendi. These pages explain that Bahá’u’lláh revealed the book in Arabic around 1873 in ‘Akká, that it was withheld for a time before being sent to Iran, and that its laws are applied progressively. They also explain the translation's style, which follows the English Shoghi Effendi used for the roughly one-third of the text he had already translated.

sections.title: The Kitáb-i-Aqdas (¶ 1–190)
sections.keyIdea: The main text: 190 numbered paragraphs of law, exhortation and address.
sections.summary: The main text has no chapters; the authorized edition numbers it in 190 paragraphs. It moves between the laws of obligatory prayer (from ¶ 6) and fasting (¶ 16–17), personal status such as marriage, divorce and inheritance, social ordinances, and addresses to kings, religious leaders and the peoples of the world. It establishes the House of Justice in every city (¶ 30) and directs believers after Bahá’u’lláh's passing to turn to “Him Whom God hath purposed” (¶ 121, ¶ 174), which Bahá’ís understand as the appointment of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá and the basis of the Covenant.

sections.title: Some texts supplementary to the Kitáb-i-Aqdas
sections.keyIdea: Later passages by Bahá’u’lláh that add to or explain the book's provisions.
sections.summary: This section collects passages from Tablets revealed after the Aqdas, such as the Eighth Ishráq of the Tablet of Ishráqát, which Bahá’u’lláh said was to be counted as part of the Most Holy Book. Several concern the House of Justice and its authority to legislate on matters not in the text. They are printed separately so that readers can see which words belong to the main book.

sections.title: Questions and Answers (107 items)
sections.keyIdea: Bahá’u’lláh's replies to questions about how particular laws apply.
sections.summary: The Questions and Answers were compiled by Zaynu’l-Muqarrabín, a transcriber of Bahá’u’lláh's writings, from answers to questions put by believers. The introduction calls them an invaluable appendix to the Aqdas. They settle details such as festival dates, prayer, fasting, marriage and inheritance shares.

sections.title: Synopsis and Codification of the Laws and Ordinances
sections.keyIdea: A topical outline of the laws, first prepared under Shoghi Effendi.
sections.summary: The Synopsis and Codification arranges the laws of the Aqdas and its supplementary texts under headings such as prayer, fasting, personal status and miscellaneous laws. It lets a reader find every ordinance on one subject without searching the whole text. It is an aid to study and does not replace the text itself.

sections.title: Notes and key to Shoghi Effendi's translations
sections.keyIdea: 194 explanatory notes, keyed to paragraphs, plus a list of earlier translations.
sections.summary: The notes explain terms, historical references and how particular laws are understood or applied, citing ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá, Shoghi Effendi and the Universal House of Justice. Each note links back to its paragraph. A final key lists the passages Shoghi Effendi had already translated and where they first appeared.

faq.q: Where can I read the Kitáb-i-Aqdas in English?
faq.a: The authorized English translation, first published in 1992, is available free in the Bahá’í Reference Library at bahai.org, with PDF, DOCX and HTML downloads. That edition includes the supplementary texts, Questions and Answers, the Synopsis and Codification and the notes. Readers should use it rather than older partial or unofficial renderings, since the Bahá’í community treats it as the authoritative English text.

faq.q: Are all the laws of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas in force today?
faq.a: No, not all of them. The introduction to the authorized edition explains that Bahá’u’lláh provided for the progressive application of His laws, because the society for which some were designed will come about only gradually. Some laws, such as obligatory prayer and fasting, are treated as binding now for Bahá’ís where they do not conflict with civil law; others are applied only when the Universal House of Justice decides.

faq.q: What is the role of the Universal House of Justice in relation to the Aqdas?
faq.a: The Aqdas ordains Houses of Justice, and Bahá’ís understand the Universal House of Justice, first elected in 1963, as the institution it anticipates. According to the edition's introduction, it may legislate on matters not revealed in the book and may change its own legislation, but it cannot alter laws explicitly laid down in the text. Authoritative interpretation of the text itself was assigned to ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá and then to Shoghi Effendi.

faq.q: How long is the Kitáb-i-Aqdas?
faq.a: The main text is 190 short paragraphs and can be read in about an hour and a half. The full authorized volume, with the supplementary texts, 107 Questions and Answers, the Synopsis and 194 notes, is several times longer. Most readers find the notes necessary for understanding specific laws.

practice.title: Reading a law with its note
practice.instruction: Read ¶ 1–5 of the main text in the authorized edition. Then choose one law from ¶ 6–20, read it, and write down in one sentence what you think it requires. Next, follow the note number attached to that paragraph and read the note and any related Question and Answer. Write a second sentence recording what the note added or corrected, and which voice (main text, question, note) each piece of information came from.

facts.origin: Revealed by Bahá’u’lláh in ‘Akká (Acre), Ottoman Palestine, around 1873
facts.form: 190 paragraphs in the main text; the authorized edition adds supplementary texts, 107 Questions and Answers, a Synopsis and Codification and 194 notes
